title: Beach Culture no. 5
lede: An issue of the surf and culture magazine that Carson art-directed before Ray Gun, with mirrored, overlapping, and cropped display type.
summary: Painted cover by Gary Baseman; inside, mirrored giant letters across the gutter and spaced capitals overprinted on a blurred photo. David Carson, 1991.

source.label: Display Graphic Design Collection: Beach Culture No. 5, Feb/March 1991

evidence.note: Inspected five photographs (1600 × 1280 each) of one copy offered by Display in scratchpad copies: the cover and four interior spreads. The copy has no collection number. Not stored.

styles.note: Precursor and partial fit: the layouts break the grid and overlap type as in Ray Gun, but the letterforms are clean and the grounds are mostly plain paper.

context: Carson became art director of Beach Culture in 1989; the magazine ended after six issues. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Carson_(graphic_designer)).

Display lists the issue as no. 5, February/March 1991, edited by Neil Feineman and published by Surfer Publishing Group, with a cover by Gary Baseman. It quotes Steven Heller: “Letter forms overlap, overprint, smash, and are otherwise covered by black, mortised, random bands.” [Display](https://bookstore.thisisdisplay.org/products/beach-culture-no-5-feb-march-1991-david-carson).

Display quotes Carson (Under Pressure, 2018) calling Beach Culture his best editorial work and saying he was already doing the Ray Gun kind of work there. [Display](https://bookstore.thisisdisplay.org/products/beach-culture-no-5-feb-march-1991-david-carson).
observed: The cover is a red, black, and white brush painting by Gary Baseman. The masthead is blue condensed slab capitals, stacked, with a yellow box around the issue number.
A cover line, “life on the pro tour”, is set in blue lowercase letters stepped down the page one or two at a time.
The “hanging at carmine st.” spread sets huge grey and black sans-serif letters mirrored and upside down across the gutter; one word is cut in half by the page edge.
“the song chant of the bush by wayne lynch” is a heavy lowercase sans-serif with wide word spaces, cropped by a photograph at the gutter.
A spread titled “romeo void” spaces single large letters in cells of thin rules; body text is a small typewriter-like face in narrow columns, next to blurred halftone images.
“GRACELAND, PARADISE GARDEN, AND ST. COCA COLA” is set in widely spaced capitals whose lines overlap each other over a blurred photograph.
interpretation: Beach Culture shows the step before grunge: the layout is already broken and intuitive, but the type is not yet damaged. Its wide letterspacing is closer to [New Wave typography](style:new-wave-typography), which marks the boundary between the two styles.
borrow: Mirror or invert one oversized word so it reads as shape before it reads as text.
Let two lines of spaced capitals overlap over a blurred photograph.

rights.statement: No image is stored. David Carson is living, so the design is in copyright. Photographs by their sources. The cover painting is by Gary Baseman.
